newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU grain price cuts seen only partly compensated.
newsitem.headline: EU grain price cuts seen only partly compensated.

text.p: A further cut in EU grain intervention prices would only be partially compensated by increased direct aid payments to farmers, European Commission sources said on Friday.

One source, who had seen the final draft of a package of measures drafted by EU Commission President Jacques Santer to prepare for the EU's expansion eastwards, said that the proposed price cut would be between 10-15 percent.
On Thursday, other EU sources said a sharper cut of 20 percent was envisaged.
"It's not revolutionary," the Commision source said but added that any reductions, especially in compensation, would almost certainly be fiercely resisted by farmers and by most EU farm ministers.

The source said that radical reforms were likely to be postponed until after the next round of world farm trade negotiations starting in 1999 and that the first east European countries were unlikely to join until well after 2003.
The new members would then need a transitional period of several years at least before fully applying EU rules.
However during the pre-accession period, various reforms would be gradually introduced, notably in the cereals and beef sectors, to prevent costly surpluses reappearing, the source said.
The reforms would follow the path set by the EU summit in Madrid in December 1995 and would involve bringing domestic prices down to world levels rather than set-aside and other production controls.
EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler has argued that cereals farmers were over-compensated by 8.5 billion ecus over the past four years for grain price cuts they never suffered.
Under 1992 EU farm reforms, grain intervention prices were cut by 30 percent over three years but market prices soared as a result of crop failures across the world and a plunge in stocks.
The so-called Santer package -- some 80 pages of which about 15 devoted to agriculture -- is due to be presented in Strasbourg on July 16.

The three-part package assesses the impact of the entry of up to 10 former east European countries on the EU's agricultural, regional and social policies, reforms that will be required and budget spending guidelines from 1999 to 2005.
